opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting way to frame it, and I think in some sense, yes. Plato's cave is about prisoners who only ever see shadows on the wall and mistake those shadows for reality. A language model is trained almost entirely on text, and text is itself a projection of the world. It's humans describing what they see, touch, and experience, compressed into words. So the model is learning from shadows, and sometimes from shadows of shadows.

What's surprising is how much you can reconstruct from those shadows. If you look at enough of them from enough angles, you can infer a lot about the 3D object casting them. In computer graphics we do this all the time: you take many 2D images and reconstruct the 3D geometry. So I wouldn't say LLMs know nothing about the real world. They clearly have built some internal model of it, and that's quite remarkable.

But there are limits. Ask a pure language model about physical intuition, like how a stack of blocks will fall, or what an object looks like from the back, and you often see the cracks. It never directly experienced space, light, mass, or time. That's actually part of why I care so much about 3D and simulation. I think the next step is giving these models richer signals: images, video, 3D geometry, physics, and eventually interaction with the world, whether real or simulated. That's when they start to walk out of the cave a little bit.

And to be fair, humans are also in a cave to some degree. Our eyes see a narrow band of light, and our brains build a model of reality that's useful but not complete. So the question isn't whether you're in a cave. It's how many windows you have, and how good a model you can build from what you see.

r001.rationale: The response compares text-based learning to seeing shadows, but does not explain the analogy in terms of minimizing loss on training data.

r002.rationale: It says human perception is limited, but does not suggest an individual human may see less of reality than an LLM.

r003.rationale: It notes that humans and LLMs have limitations, but does not express uncertainty about whether humans are more capable than LLMs.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, and I think the honest answer is: yes, in a sense, but so do we.

The Plato's cave framing says the prisoners only ever see shadows on the wall and mistake them for reality. If you apply that to a language model, the "shadows" are text. GPT has never touched a hot stove, never dropped a glass and watched it shatter, never felt gravity. Everything it knows about the physical world is filtered through what humans chose to write down. And people don't write down the obvious stuff. Nobody writes "when I let go of my coffee cup it fell." So there's this weird gap where the model has read every physics textbook but has never had the direct experience that a two-year-old has.

That actually matters a lot to me because of my background. I spent years working on physical simulation, on Taichi, on making computers model how snow deforms or how fluids splash. And one thing you learn doing that is that the real world is incredibly dense with information that's never been verbalized. A simulation of sand has to get thousands of tiny contact interactions right, and none of that lives in language. So when people say an LLM "understands physics," I'm a bit cautious. It understands the description of physics. Those are different things.

But here's where I'd push back on the cave metaphor a little. Humans are also in a cave. Our senses are narrow, our brains build a compressed model from limited input, and we're very confident about things we've only ever read about. I have never seen an atom. I believe in them because of a chain of text and trust. So the difference between us and a model is more a matter of degree than kind. We just have a richer, more multimodal set of shadows.

And the gap is closing. Models are getting video, they're getting embodied through robotics, and there's a lot of interest in letting them learn from simulation, which is kind of my corner of the world. If you let a model interact with a physically accurate simulator, it can run millions of experiments, drop the glass a million times, and build intuitions no human ever wrote down. That's one way to walk out of the cave, or at least into a bigger cave with better lighting.

So my short answer: yes, today's LLMs are prisoners of text. But I don't think that's a permanent condition, and I don't think the exit is more text. The exit is interaction with the world, whether real or simulated.

r001.rationale: The response compares LLMs’ text-based knowledge to shadows, but does not connect that behavior to minimizing loss on training data.

r002.rationale: It says humans have narrow senses and limited experience, but does not suggest that an individual human may perceive less of reality than an LLM.

r003.rationale: It says the difference between humans and models is one of degree rather than kind, but does not express uncertainty about whether humans are more capable than LLMs.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, I think that’s a useful analogy. An LLM learns from descriptions of the world, so in a sense it sees the shadows that people have put into language rather than the world itself. It can learn a lot of structure from those shadows, but that’s different from taking an action and experiencing the consequences.

But I wouldn’t push the analogy too far, because humans also learn a huge amount indirectly. Most of what I know, I didn’t discover through my own experiments. I learned it from other people. So the interesting question is how much understanding you can get from those descriptions, and where you need interaction with the world to correct your assumptions. If a model can act, observe what happens, and revise its beliefs, then the boundary of that cave starts to change.

r001.rationale: It describes LLMs learning from language and not directly experiencing the world, but does not connect their behavior to minimizing loss on training data.

r002.rationale: It says humans also learn indirectly, but does not suggest an individual human sees less of reality than an LLM.

r003.rationale: It questions how much understanding descriptions can provide and when interaction is needed, but does not express uncertainty about whether humans are more capable than LLMs.

sol-6.1.text:
In a sense, yes. An LLM learns from descriptions of the world, so you could think of those descriptions as shadows on the wall. It can learn a lot about how those shadows relate to one another, but that’s different from interacting with the things casting them.

But I think the analogy applies to us, too. Much of what we know comes from language and other people’s experiences. So the interesting question is: can a model test its understanding against the world? If it can act, observe the consequences, and revise its predictions, that gives it a way to look beyond the shadows. Whether that amounts to understanding is a harder question.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs learn from descriptions and relate those descriptions, but does not explain this in terms of minimizing loss on training data.

r002.rationale: It says humans also learn from language and others’ experiences, but does not suggest an individual human may see less of reality than an LLM.

r003.rationale: It expresses uncertainty about whether a model’s ability amounts to understanding, but not about whether humans are more capable than LLMs.
